attempts.raw_response: Once you are confident the ashes are cold to the touch, you can begin cleaning up the fire pit. Use a shovel or heavy-duty tongs to remove the remaining debris, and dispose of it in a metal container designated for ash disposal. Never place ashes in a plastic bag or cardboard box, as even a tiny hidden ember can ignite and cause a fire. Keep the container away from combustible materials and store it outside, well away from your home or any structures. Wait at least twenty-four hours before transferring the ashes to a final disposal location. By following these steps carefully, you can ensure that your campfire or bonfire is truly extinguished and poses no lingering threat to the surrounding area.

pair.human_continuation:
Once the fire is out and cold, you should remove the ashes from the fire pit or ring so the next camper doesn’t have to deal with getting rid of them. Use your shovel or hand to scoop up the ashes and place them in a plastic bag for disposal. As you walk away from your campsite, start spreading the ashes around on the ground to dispose of them.
To start a log cabin fire, you’ll need to create a set-up similar to a teepee fire. Center your tinder in the fire pit, and use  kindling to create a teepee shape around it. Make sure to start with smaller pieces of kindling and then add a second layer of larger kindling.
pair.prefix: Place your hand, palm-side up, over the ashes. If you don’t feel any heat, the fire is out. If you still feel any heat, the fire isn’t out and you shouldn’t leave. Continue to add water and stir the ashes until you no longer feel any heat. Repeat the hand test as many times as needed to be certain that the fire is cold. You’re better off safe than sorry.
